questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Overall, I chose my study destination on the grounds of location, courses offered and earlier evaluations from other students. My greatest wish for my exchange was to experience a new culture, and when I found out, that I (i) had a housing-opportunity in Rome opening for such an experience and (ii) that the host university, at the same time, had an interesting program of courses, I was sure about choosing Rome to be my study destination.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Go on an exchange, regardless of which destination will end up being available for you.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was quite easy. The host institution was very well-prepared and good at orienting and assist in case of questions and concerns in general. The host university had made a “Handbook for International Students” introducing us to everything we needed to know before starting our exchange, during our studies at the host university, etc. This guidance was very helpful and in case the handbook didn't answer relevant questions, you could write to the Student Mobility Office and expect an answer within short time.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: As explained above, we received a very useful handbook. In addition, as explained later, you could sign yourself up for a buddy-program opening up for assistance from one of the local students.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: No.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: For me, personally, it was quite easy. As mentioned below, I was lucky to know someone who knew someone. I would recommend starting you search for housing early - and if you're using social platforms, be aware of scams.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Bear in mind the location and the distance from the university. And if you're living off campus with non-Erasmus students, you should be prepared for a possible language barrier.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was fortunate that a close friend of mine knew someone, living in Rome, who was going abroad on an exchange for the same semester. I rented his room and lived with two Italian guys, studying at the same university as me. The apartment was located in Parioli, known as one of the wealthier areas of Rome. It was quiet, clean and felt safe during dark hours. Parioli is located a bit outside of the city center, but it's the area where the headquarters of the university are located, including the three faculties you are to study at as a law student. Even though located a bit outside, the city center is easy reachable in only 10 minutes with several busses, the U-train and trams. I would highly recommend living in Parioli – but also living with locals. Throughout my exchange, my roomies introduced to me to anything from the Italian culture by inviting me to family-gatherings, to the Italian cuisine and the procedures on our university. A great experience being housed as such throughout my exchange!

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: See below.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
Before leaving home, the administration of the host university will send you an e-mail explaining the registration process. They will publish an Excel-sheet with a list of all courses for the whole university for the upcoming academic year. Be aware, that this list also consists of courses on other faculties. You will be able to look up all relevant courses on a platform describing the course, the professor and the exam method. 

The process begins with registering yourself at (typically) five courses on 6 ECTS – this will be done shortly after your exchange spot is confirmed. It's important to check the time-schedules of the chosen courses, so no timetables overlaps! Within one month you will receive a confirmation on your registration. Unfortunately, one of my five courses got cancelled, why I only was assigned 24 ECTS to begin with. A little while after the initial confirmation, the host university will open a second registration-period, where you can find a fifth course suiting your timetable. 

Because of the possibility of not being confirmed on all of your initial courses, I would recommend getting a pre-approval on at least 60 ECTS from the University of Copenhagen. By doing so, you have more courses to choose in the second registration-period. 

When you arrive in Rome and start at the host university, they let you “course-shop” for the first two weeks, so you can try your chosen courses and – if you're not satisfied – choose some other courses to be finally determined two weeks after the start of the semester.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The host university will send you a full guide explaining all necessary steps to be aware of. They're very good at answering on e-mails in case of any uncertainties. In addition, you're assigned an exchange-buddy from the host university who will assist you and answer any questions that may occur.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: This is explained above. In the end – after trying different courses in the first two weeks of the semester – I got assigned to all of the five courses I wanted. There was no problem at all. In some of the courses only 20 students attended – in others 60 students, so overall, I think the host university runs the greater part of the initially available courses.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: See above about things to be aware of during the registration. Stay calm during the process – it can be a bit challenging not knowing your final courses at semester start. This is completely different compared to the University of Copenhagen, but in the end, everything will turn out in the way you want it to be.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: See below.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level of the courses differs a lot. Some professors were surprisingly bad at English pronunciation and, unfortunately, that had an impact on the overall outcome of the given courses. In some courses, the professors were a bit unspecific with regards to readings and assignments, and in that way, the level of the given courses were up to the students to decide – for example through own proposals of readings and such. In other courses, the professors expected a lot; that we were well-prepared, ready to answer unknown questions throughout the lectures and tuned to day-to-day changes. Overall, I would say, that the level of courses is higher at the University of Copenhagen, but with that said, you'll still have a great outcome academically.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The style of teaching at the host university is very different from the one at the University of Copenhagen. First, there's a completely different relationship between the students and a professor. A professor is typically very authoritarian and conversations with a professor occurs in a very formal language. Secondly, the assessment method in each course differs a lot, and you need to be aware of how you're assessed in each course. In one course, you're assessed solely based on one test or a written assessment, in another course, you're assessed 10 percent on presence, 20 percent on active participation, 20 percent on an oral presentation and 50 percent on a final exam – written or oral depending on whether you have participated or not. You need to be aware of the fact, that many of the decisions are made solely by the professor in each course and not administratively. Finally, be prepared of a relatively heavy workload, given that the courses are only 6 ECTS, and lastly - prepare yourself on being secure in speaking english. You'll use a lot in class, and if you are to have any oral exams, they will typically be held with the whole class present while being examined.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Climate Justice (M479)
Data Protection Law (M389)
EU Law Before Courts: Rights and Procedures (M471)
European Private Law (AD4)
Media Law (M469)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would highly recommend Data Protection Law. It's a very interesting course and the professor is very competent. His teaching method is very different from the one at the University of Copenhagen, and the overall workload is quite huge being a 6 ECTS-course. Nevertheless, attending the course will help you understand the legal framework around Data Protection both in the Union but also in other parts of the world, and when finishing the course, you'll the needed amount of knowledge to feel more secure in working with personal data. 

If you're interested in Human Rights Law, both Climate Justice and Media Law are two great courses as well. They'll introduce you to a great part of the European human rights framework, and in the courses, you'll work and deal with very contemporary topics.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
Expensive monthly bills for water, heat, electricity, etc.

You will end up spending money on a taxi home during night hours.

Make sure you have considered that you may need to go home to Denmark for a weekend or two during the exchange-period.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: It's, generally speaking, very cheap to eat out at restaurants compared to buying groceries. It's also affordable both experiencing cultural sites as an EU Under 25-citizen. And using the railway for weekend trips didn't cost as much as expected.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: See below.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Both the host university, the ESN-Network and the Erasmus Roma Association arranged everything from training, sport practices and tournaments to cultural exhibitions and city tours. ESN is a network connected solely to the host university while the Erasmus Roma Association is linked to all international students on all universities in Rome. Both organizations offer discounts on everything from dinner places to museums besides organizing such things themselves. Both organizations also arrange day- and weekend-trips outside of Rome. Be aware that every EU-citizen under the age of 25 will get access to all cultural sites in Italy for only 2 Euros.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Participate in whatever you're just considering. When participating in these non-academic activities, regardless of what it is, you will get to know new people, and this is a part of the whole idea behind going on an exchange.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Italy has an amazing railway-system. All the big cities around Italy are connected to Rome with train, and a train-ticket will often be affordable, since the two major companies operates with discounts for students and “Under 25”. I would highly recommend taking weekend trips to everything from Venice and Milan in the northern part of Italy, Pisa and Lucca in Tuscany to the Amalfi coast and Naples in the south. There are also great places to visit for a day-trip – the Vesuvius Volcano, Tivoli and Lago de Bracciano. All amazing places if you like nature and hiking.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
It takes time - but it will take time no matter where you're going. 

Italians are, first of all, very proud of their language. Many people in the elder as well as the younger generation doesn't speak english, and this can be a it challenging sometimes. Nevertheless, Italians are very easy-going and they often take things as they may come - no one really operates with a calendar and plans for the future. This is very different from Denmark, but you'll quickly fall into the Italian way of living - it's so great to start you day off by drinking a cappuccino on your own, local café around the corner and spontaneously go out for an Aperol after class.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Italians may seem a bit reserved because of their difficulties with English,  but they are not - at all. Be open and use Google Translate as a tool for communication - both by message and in person. With this said, Luiss is a very internationally oriented university, and many of the local students will be good at speaking english. Just say hi and ask them, if you have any questions.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Explained above.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Also explained above.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Be open, be patient and be excited.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Download TicketAppy for public transportation and order your groceries and dinner on Deliveroo when having a day off - always offering many different things at fair prices.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Cliché, but everything. Just go.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Meeting the Italian hospital system. Make sure, that you have a good insurance by choosing the company, where you have your other insurances :)

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: No.

questions.answer: Yes
